implementation_notes: Modern C++ keeps the mutex as a private member (usually mutable) and never calls lock()/unlock() directly: the standard library's RAII wrappers - std::lock_guard for one lock, std::scoped_lock (C++17) or std::lock for several - acquire in the constructor and release in the destructor on every exit path, including exceptions (cppreference notes std::mutex is usually not accessed directly). The classic pattern survives as the type-level contract: any type providing lock()/unlock()/try_lock() models the C++11 named requirements BasicLockable/Lockable and can be used with those wrappers and with std::condition_variable_any.
pitfalls: Forgetting the guard and calling lock()/unlock() by hand reintroduces every exception/early-return leak the wrappers remove.
Acquiring two mutexes without std::scoped_lock/std::lock deadlocks under opposite ordering; the multi-lock helpers exist for exactly this case.
A std::mutex that is copied or moved does not compile, but slicing through a base class or a by-value parameter can still duplicate the guarded state (the lock stays behind with the original object).

variants.name: Object models the Lockable named requirement (published lock interface)
variants.implementation_notes: The classic POSA-style shape: the object itself satisfies the C++11 Lockable named requirement - public lock(), unlock() and try_lock() - so collaborators can hand it to std::lock_guard, std::scoped_lock, std::lock, std::unique_lock or std::condition_variable_any exactly like a std::mutex, and the RAII wrappers keep the release path safe even though the lock is published. Choose it when the lock must be a first-class collaborator (generic locking utilities, adapters such as a no-op or logging lock wrapping the real mutex); prefer the private-member variant when only the object's own methods ever lock.
pitfalls: Omitting try_lock() silently breaks the Lockable requirement (std::lock and std::scoped_lock fall back to BasicLockable only with effort, and generic algorithms may not compile as intended).
A published lock is only as safe as its exception behaviour: lock() that throws after acquiring, or unlock() that throws, leaves the guard contract violated.
Adapters must forward try_lock faithfully; a no-op lock that reports failure where a real lock would succeed changes the victim's semantics, not just performance.
